Teen Drug Use Down

Saturday December 20

WASHINGTON, Dec. 20 (UPI) _ A new report the Department of Health and Human Services indicates a decline in drug use by eighth-graders.

In his weekly radio address Saturday, President Clinton says it is the first time since 1991 that a government study has found a decline in teenage drug use.

Clinton said: ``Today's eighth-graders are less likely to have used drugs over the past year, and just as important, they are more likely to disapprove of drug use.''

Retired Gen. Barry McCaffrey, the White House drug czar, pointed to a Harvard University study indicating that parents' biggest concern is ``their children and drugs.''

McCaffrey added, ``So many of us believe when parents get engaged, when media attention or other reasons cause them to focus on their children and drug use, not somebody else's kids, they get engaged and the children's attitudes start responding.''

The retired Army general said statistics show it is most important to keep drugs, including alcohol and tobacco, away from children aged nine to 19.

He added, ``a 12-year-old regularly using marijuana by the way, he's probably also abusing alcohol and smoking cigarettes is mathematically in trouble.''

Survey Finds Teen Drug Use Steady

By Eun-Kyung Kim
Associated Press Writer
WASHINGTON (AP) -- Drug use among teen-agers remained stable last year and more adolescents are starting to disapprove of such activity, according to an annual survey released today by the Clinton administration.

The use of illegal drugs among eighth graders was steady from 1996 to 1997, with the exceptions of marijuana, cigarettes and heroin, which showed a slight decrease in use, according to the report by the Department of Health and Human Services.

There also was some stability in the number of 10th- and 12th-graders who used drugs in the past year or month, the survey found. However, reported daily use of marijuana by high school seniors rose from 4.9 percent in 1996 to 5.8 percent this year.

In a statement echoed by President Clinton and a Republican spokesmen in separate radio messages, HHS Secretary Donna Shalala said: ``The possible slowdown of illicit drug use among young people is encouraging, even though rates of use remain unacceptably high. All of us, especially parents and teachers, need to redouble our efforts to make young people understand that drug abuse is illegal, dangerous and wrong.''

``The most effective strategy we have against drugs begins at home. It's a fight that can be won at kitchen tables all across America,'' Clinton said in his weekly radio appearance. ``This holiday season, as we spend some hard-earned time with our families, I urge all parents to sit down with their children, as Hillary and I have done, and share a simple and important lesson: Drugs are dangerous, drugs are wrong and drugs can kill.''

Rep. Rob Portman, R-Ohio, also encouraged parents to be more aggressive in warning their children about the dangers of drugs.

``This is a powerful new tool -- because we now know that parents can reduce the chances of their children using drugs by more than 30 percent if they would simply talk to their kids about the dangers,'' Portman said in the GOP radio address.

Portman said that while the HHS survey may show some improvement over last year's numbers, ``it still represents a failing grade'' because drug abuse among adolescents remains high.

``Teen-age drug abuse has more than doubled over the past five years and it has grown to unacceptable levels,'' he said. ``This is not the time to take comfort in a report that documents that increase. Rather, we must redouble our efforts to address the drug crisis and send the clear and consistent message at every level -- from the White House to the family dinner table -- that drug use is dangerous and wrong.''

Clinton and Portman both pointed to government efforts to help the process along, including the approval of $195 million in funding for a media campaign against drugs.

``Our goal is to make sure that every time a child turns on the TV, listens to the radio or surfs the Internet, he or she will get the powerful message that drugs can destroy your life,'' Clinton said.

According to the HHS survey, the percentage of eighth graders who disapproved of occasional use of marijuana increased for the first time since 1991. It rose from 76.5 percent in 1996 to 78.1 percent this year. The disapproval rate among eighth graders of regular marijuana use, occasional cocaine use, heavy drinking and frequent cigarette smoking also increased.

Adolescent attitudes about drug use are key predictors of increases and decreases in the subsequent use of drugs, health experts said.

``The apparent shift in attitudes and leveling off of drug use among eighth graders provides additional evidence that anti-drug prevention activities may be taking hold with young people,'' said Dr. Alan I. Leshner, director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, the agency that funded the HHS study.
